primary.thesis: The KMT starts from a dominant local base: after the 2022 cycle it held about 14 of the 22 listed seats, including Taipei, New Taipei, Taoyuan, Taichung, Keelung and most northern, central and offshore counties. The DPP's reliable base is the south: Tainan, Kaohsiung, Pingtung, Chiayi County and, at times, Penghu. Several things favour the KMT in the 2026 cycle: local races usually turn on local issues, the ruling party usually does badly at midterm, the DPP's mass recall campaign against KMT legislators failed in 2025, and the KMT and TPP are coordinating so they do not split the opposition vote. The DPP would need about 11 seats to tie, which would mean flipping several northern or central municipalities as well as keeping all of its southern base. The TPP has at most one or two realistic races, such as Hsinchu City, so it cannot come close to the top. Ties go to the party whose English name comes first alphabetically, which is the DPP. That is only a small edge, because the KMT is expected to win by a wide margin. Mechanism: many KMT incumbents running again or handing over to successors, together with opposition coordination, should give the KMT the most wins. It may even pass 12 wins before every count is final, at which point no other party can catch it.

basket.reason: Incumbency across 13-14 seats, KMT-TPP coordination and midterm anti-incumbent swing against the ruling DPP make the KMT the structural favourite for the plurality.
To win or tie, the DPP needs roughly 11 of 22. That would mean holding the entire southern base and flipping several KMT-held municipalities or counties, which it has not done since 2014.
The TPP contests only a handful of seats, and some of those it concedes to the KMT under the cooperation deal. It cannot plausibly lead the count.

failure_narrative: The basket loses if the DPP reaches at least as many wins as the KMT; because of the alphabetical tiebreak, a tie is enough. The most likely way this happens is that the election becomes a vote on national sovereignty rather than local issues. A sharp act of PRC coercion before the vote could do it, such as blockade-style drills, a quarantine of the offshore islands or open interference in the campaign. So could KMT chair Cheng Li-wun's pro-Beijing positioning becoming the main campaign issue. Either could produce a rally-around-the-DPP swing across the swing municipalities: Taoyuan, Taichung, New Taipei, Hsinchu, Changhua, Yilan and Keelung. A second route is that KMT-TPP coordination collapses, splitting the opposition vote in three-way races. Rebel independents who count for no party could add to this, as could a big scandal among KMT incumbents. That would leave the DPP level with the KMT or ahead of it.
hedge_thesis: The primary thesis fails mainly when Taiwan's local election turns into a vote on security because Beijing escalates. In those same worlds the tension would spread to Taiwan's neighbours and allies. Japan would likely harden its security stance, continuing the China-Japan dispute over Taiwan contingency remarks that began in late 2025. Tokyo would speed up defence spending, and Japanese defence contractors would gain. The US would be likely to fast-track arms sales, and the Philippines would draw closer to the US under their alliance. The mechanism is that one shared cause, visible PRC military or coercive pressure, both swings Taiwanese voters toward the DPP and pushes up defence procurement and defence-equity prices in Japan and the US. So a hedge on East Asian defence build-up outside Taiwan should pay off in exactly the worlds where the KMT loses its plurality.
